cards.q: What is CIDR and why was it introduced?
cards.a: CIDR (Classless Inter-Domain Routing) replaced traditional fixed IPv4 classes with arbitrary prefix lengths written as address/prefix-length (e.g. 192.168.10.0/24); it provides flexible address allocation, route aggregation/summarization, classless routing that carries prefix/mask info, and more efficient use of IPv4 space.

cards.q: What does the /x in CIDR notation specify?
cards.a: It specifies the number of leading 1-bits in the subnet mask (the prefix length), which determines how many bits identify the network and how many remain for hosts; for example /20 = 255.255.240.0, and any prefix is valid regardless of historical Class A/B/C boundaries.

cards.q: What are the main benefits of CIDR?
cards.a: Flexible allocation to actual network requirements, address efficiency (smaller prefixes like /27 or /28 avoid oversized subnets), route aggregation of multiple contiguous networks into one summary route, smaller routing tables, classless routing with prefix-length information, and supernetting.

cards.q: How do you summarize four contiguous /24 networks?
cards.a: 192.168.0.0/24 through 192.168.3.0/24 share the common prefix 192.168.0.0/22, because a /22 contains four /24 networks; this is an exact summary when the networks are contiguous and correctly aligned on the /22 boundary.

No; a /22 has a block size of 4 in the third octet (boundaries 0, 4, 8, 12...), so 192.168.0.0/22 covers .0–.3 and would include the extra 192.168.0.0/24 network; an exact representation needs more than one summary, so always check binary common prefix and alignment.

cards.q: What is supernetting and what happens to the prefix length?
cards.a: Supernetting combines multiple smaller networks into a larger CIDR prefix, for example four /24 networks become 192.168.0.0/22; the prefix becomes shorter, and a shorter prefix represents a larger address block — smaller prefix number means a larger network.

cards.q: What is the IPv4 default route and how does it behave?
cards.a: 0.0.0.0/0, the least-specific IPv4 prefix, which matches any IPv4 destination when no more-specific route exists.

cards.q: What is longest-prefix match for 10.0.0.0/8, 10.10.0.0/16, and 10.10.10.0/24 with destination 10.10.10.50?
cards.a: The router selects the route with the longest matching prefix; all three routes match 10.10.10.50, but /24 is the longest so it is preferred.

cards.q: What is a /31 prefix used for per RFC 3021?
cards.a: Point-to-point links; for example 10.0.0.0/31 contains two addresses, 10.0.0.0 and 10.0.0.1, avoiding the traditional reservation of separate network and broadcast addresses on a point-to-point link.

cards.q: What is a /32 prefix and what is it used for?
cards.a: It identifies exactly one IPv4 address, e.g. 192.168.10.50/32; common uses include loopback addresses, host-specific routes, router IDs, and specific routing entries.

cards.q: How does Cisco IOS express CIDR prefixes in configuration?
cards.a: The traditional ip address command uses dotted-decimal masks, e.g. ip address 192.168.10.1 255.255.255.224 (which is /27); a summarized static route is written ip route 192.168.0.0 255.255.252.0 10.0.0.1, representing 192.168.0.0/22 with next hop 10.0.0.1.

cards.q: What commands verify CIDR configuration and routing?
cards.a: show ip route, show ip route 192.168.0.0, show ip interface brief, and show running-config.

cards.q: Does CIDR mean that a smaller prefix number is always better?
cards.a: No; the prefix number only indicates block size — /22 is larger than /23 and /23 is larger than /24, so a shorter prefix is a larger network, which is not automatically better for every design.

cards.q: Must a network use /24 just because it was historically a Class C address?
cards.a: No; CIDR is classless, so you do not apply Class A/B/C assumptions, and prefixes like /20, /21, or /27 are perfectly valid for any address.

cards.q: Do three /24 networks automatically equal one /22?
cards.a: No; a /22 contains four /24 networks, so the block size is 4 and three /24s are not enough to fill it; the summary prefix must also be correctly aligned.

cards.q: What are the address counts for /32 down to /24?
How do you compute total addresses and traditional usable hosts for prefix /x?
cards.a: Total addresses = 2^(32 − x) and traditional usable hosts = 2^(32 − x) − 2, e.g. /24 → 256/254, /26 → 64/62, /27 → 32/30, /28 → 16/14; the −2 rule has exceptions for /31 point-to-point links and /32 host routes.

cards.q: State the quick CIDR memory rules.
cards.a: CIDR = address + prefix length; shorter prefix = larger block, longer prefix = smaller block; network = IP AND mask; default route = 0.0.0.0/0; longest-prefix match means the most-specific matching route wins.
